transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what’s been bothering you or what brings you in today?

Well… it may sound a bit silly, Doctor, but it’s bridges. When I know I have to cross one and there’s no way around it, I get frightened right away, before I’m even on it. My heart starts pounding, my hands get damp on the steering wheel or the armrest, and I just get this awful rush of fear. I know it may not seem like much, but it’s been bothering me.
Is this fear limited to certain types of bridges, like high bridges, long bridges, or ones over water, or does it happen with any bridge regardless of its size or location?

It’s mostly the high ones, I suppose… especially when I can see the span ahead of me or even just notice it on the map. I know, rationally, that thousands of cars go over those bridges every day without anything happening. But to me, in that moment, it feels as if the whole thing is just… waiting to drop away underneath us. I know that probably sounds unreasonable, but that’s the feeling I get.
When you know you have to cross a high bridge, do you try to avoid it altogether, or do you go ahead and cross it even though it makes you very anxious?

I try to avoid it, yes… more than I probably should. For over two years now I’ve been planning errands and visits so I don’t have to go over the high bridges. I’ve even given up trips to San Juan and some theater nights in Seattle, which I suppose sounds a bit much.

If I absolutely have to cross one, I can do it, but only if I’ve studied the route ahead of time, picked the timing carefully, and have someone with me. And even then I’m just sitting there frightened the whole way across. Is that the sort of thing you mean?

When you feel this fear about crossing bridges, does it feel similar to any other situations where you might feel trapped, anxious, or out of control—like being in crowds, on public transportation, or being outside your home alone?

I’m not sure, Doctor… I don’t think I’ve noticed it in quite that way. Crowds or buses and things like that aren’t what comes to mind for me. It’s really the bridge itself, or knowing I’ll have to go over it.

I suppose there is a feeling of being stuck once you’re on it, but I don’t know if that’s the same thing you mean. Does that answer your question all right?

When you're on the bridge or thinking about crossing it, do you ever worry that you might have a panic attack — like a sudden, intense wave of fear that peaks quickly and might make you feel like you can't escape or lose control?

I’m not sure I’d call it that exactly, Doctor… I don’t want to overstate it. But yes, when I realize the bridge crossing really can’t be avoided, it comes on very suddenly. My heart starts pounding, and my hands get damp on the steering wheel or the armrest before we’re even on the bridge.

It’s a terrible rush of fear, really. I suppose it does feel like I can’t get away from it once it starts. Is that what you mean by a panic attack?
Have you ever experienced these sudden, intense waves of fear or panic in situations other than when you're about to cross a bridge?

Not that I can really think of, Doctor. I don’t want to say “never” if I’m forgetting something, but it doesn’t seem to happen to me in ordinary places or other situations.

It’s when there’s a bridge coming up—especially a high one—that I notice that sudden rush. Otherwise, I think I’m mostly all right. Does that make sense?
When you know in advance that you’ll need to cross a high bridge, do you start feeling anxious well before you actually get there—like hours or even days ahead of time?

Yes… I think I do, Doctor. I try not to make too much of it, because I know perfectly well thousands of cars go over those bridges every day and nothing happens.

But if I see a high bridge marked on the map, or I can see the span coming up through the windshield, I start getting uneasy before we’re even there. It’s not very sensible, I know, but it feels as if the whole thing is just… waiting to drop away under us.

Does that answer what you were asking?

When you start feeling anxious about crossing a high bridge in advance, does that anxiety usually go away once you've successfully avoided the bridge, or does it tend to persist regardless of whether you cross it or not?

Usually it eases if I know I’ve avoided it, yes… I suppose that’s the honest answer. I feel relieved once the route is changed and I know we won’t have to go over the bridge.

Though, I should admit, it’s gotten to where I plan around it quite a bit. For more than two years now I’ve arranged errands and visits so I don’t have to cross certain bridges. I’ve given up trips to San Juan and even some theater nights in Seattle, which sounds a little foolish when I say it out loud.

And if I absolutely have to cross one, I need the route looked at ahead of time, the timing to feel right, and someone with me. Even then I’m frightened the whole way across. I hope that’s the sort of thing you’re asking about.

When you’re on a bridge or thinking about crossing one, do you ever feel a sudden, intense wave of fear that makes you feel like you might lose control or be overwhelmed, even if you’re not in immediate danger?

Yes… yes, I think that’s fair to say. I don’t want to overstate it, but when it becomes clear that I can’t avoid the bridge, I get this awful rush of fear right away.

My heart starts pounding, and my hands get damp—on the steering wheel if I’m driving, or on the armrest if I’m not. And that can happen even before we’re actually on the bridge. It feels very overwhelming in the moment, even though I know, rationally, there isn’t some immediate danger. Is that the kind of thing you mean?

Can you think of any other specific situations—besides crossing high bridges—where you feel a similar level of fear or need to avoid them, such as being in open spaces, being away from home, or being in places where escape might be difficult?

No, I don’t think so… not in the same way, anyway.

I mean, I suppose I prefer to be comfortable and know where I’m going, but I haven’t really noticed that kind of fear with open places or just being away from home. It’s really the high bridges that seem to set it off.

If I’m missing something you mean by “escape might be difficult,” you can tell me, but nothing else is coming to mind the way the bridges do.
